diagnosis: Hemoperitoneum from a Ruptured Ovarian Cyst

patient.key: Sudden onset severe abdominal pain, vomiting, right shoulder pain (Kehr sign), tachycardia 120, BP 110/70 trending down. Sexually active. Guarding and severe tenderness, worse in lower quadrant. Hemorrhagic shock from intraperitoneal bleed.

physicalExam.abdomen: General tenderness, worse in lower quadrants, guarding, severe tenderness

missedOrders.why: Must differentiate ruptured ovarian cyst from ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Same presentation: sudden severe pain, hemoperitoneum, Kehr sign, shock. Both go to OR but the surgeon needs to know what they're walking into. An empty Î²-hCG confirms ovarian cyst.
Hemoperitoneum means blood loss. Hemoglobin drops, oxygen-carrying capacity drops. Simple non-invasive monitoring.
Pre-operative clearance. She's going to the OR. Every surgical patient needs an EKG. The tachycardia could be hemorrhagic shock or could unmask an arrhythmia.

missedOrders.why: Pre-operative. She's actively hemorrhaging â€” you need blood available BEFORE she crashes on the table. Rh typing matters if she's Rh-negative and pregnant (which you don't know until Î²-hCG returns).
Dropping hematocrit, hypotension, symptomatic. She's bleeding into her peritoneal cavity. Fluids buy time. PRBCs carry oxygen â€” the thing you're actually losing.

Severe pain from hemoperitoneum. Do NOT use ketorolac or any NSAID â€” antiplatelet effect worsens active hemorrhage. Also contraindicated perioperatively and in hemodynamic compromise. IV opioids are the only correct choice for pain here.

shouldHaveAvoided.why: Antiplatelet effect worsens active intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Also contraindicated in perioperative setting and hemodynamic compromise. Use IV opioids only.

pathophysiology.ovarianCyst: Functional ovarian cysts â€” follicular and corpus luteum â€” occur in menstruating women aged 18-35. Usually asymptomatic. Rupture causes sudden sharp pain with no typical pattern.
pathophysiology.rightOvaryBias: The right ovary ruptures more often than the left â€” anatomic proximity to the appendix + differential blood supply.
pathophysiology.riskFactors: Anticoagulation therapy, abdominal trauma. Most ruptures have no clear trigger.
pathophysiology.bleedingSpectrum: Variable â€” from trace free fluid to massive hemoperitoneum and hypovolemic shock (this case).
pathophysiology.kehrSign: Blood pools under the right hemidiaphragm â†’ phrenic nerve irritation (C3-C5) â†’ referred pain to right shoulder. Classic for intraperitoneal blood â€” think ectopic, ovarian cyst rupture, splenic rupture.
pathophysiology.surgicalIndications: Large peritoneal fluid on US + severe pain + dropping hematocrit + unstable vitals = OR. Most ovarian cyst ruptures are managed conservatively with observation and analgesia.

teachingPoints: 26F with sudden severe pelvic pain and shock = ectopic until ruled out AND ovarian cyst rupture. Î²-hCG distinguishes them. Same surgical urgency, different surgical plan.
Kehr sign (right shoulder pain) = free blood under the diaphragm. Phrenic nerve (C3-C5). Always intraperitoneal bleed.
Never NSAIDs in active hemorrhage â€” antiplatelet effect compounds the problem. IV opioids only.
Type and screen before they hit the OR. PRBCs if actively hemorrhaging. Don't wait for the Hb to drop further.
Most ovarian cyst ruptures don't need surgery â€” observation + analgesia. This one needed it because of hemodynamic instability, large hemoperitoneum, dropping hematocrit.
Right ovary ruptures more than left. If the pain is right-sided and the appendix is nearby, US sorts it out.
Pre-op bundle for any hemorrhaging patient: type and screen, EKG, NPO, IV access (2 large-bore), consents.
